newsitem.title: USA: Lynch puts stocks to 10-year old kid test.
newsitem.headline: Lynch puts stocks to 10-year old kid test.

text.p: Famed mutual fund manager Peter Lynch said Saturday that the trick to buying a good company stock is the 10-year-old child test.
"Literally, if you can't explain to a 10-year old, in three minutes or less, why you bought the stock, you're not going to win. That's a good test," Lynch told an investment conference in Boston.

The best-selling author of stock-picking books, who turned Fidelity Investments' Magellan Fund into the largest and one of the top-performing mutual funds during his 13-year tenure, said investors need only a few simple rules to trade stocks.
Spending as much as 13 minutes a year trying to figure out which way the economy or interest rates are going to go is a waste of at least 10 minutes, he said.
"It would be very useful to know when a recession will start. Trying to predict the future is a total waste of time," said Lynch, currently an executive director with Fidelity.
Investors should instead take time to research five to 10 companies, perhaps in the industry in which they work, buy good firms and hold the stock for the long run.
Reading from a computer hardware manual, Lynch said the language was gobbledygook to him, and said it is critical for investors to understand the companies they are buying.
"I put money in a stock called Dunkin Donuts. I made a lot of money," he said. "You don't have to worry about low-cost Korean imports or a recession or somebody inventing a better Donut."

Lynch confessed to knowing only mathematical basics and little about cars and computers, but said it took no genius to figure Chrysler Corp. and Microsoft Corp. would have winning stocks. He met many people who loved Chrysler's minivans, and even though he does not use a personal computer, found out that Microsoft Windows was a fixture on PCs. Both stocks have performed fabulously.
And yet while he stressed knowing the corporate basics, he said the most important factor to a company's success, its management, is almost impossible for an outsider to judge.
"Don't buy a company just because they say 'good management'. I want to buy a company that any fool can run because eventually some will," he said.
Investors should shun "whisper stocks" - tips heard from neighbours or friends - and said he has lost 20 out of 20 times when he bought a so-called longshot stock.

Lynch said he has never bought an option or shorted a stock, and he warned against buying or selling a stock just because it has gone up or down. Stocks are volatile, he said, and the average stock listed on the New York Stock Exchange fluctuates 50 percent between its annual high and low.
Rather, investors should remind themselves why they bought the stock, review the company's fundamentals, and then stick with their strategy regardless of the economy or the broad stock market.
"There are good companies out there. They are looking for you. They are in your industry," he said. "You only need a few every decade."
